title: Did dancing shape the beat of jazz?
summary: Steiner suggests dancing drew out rhythmic jazz; Ashcraft agrees playing for dancers forced discipline.

story.theme_name: Playing for dancers: dance bands and the dances themselves
story.community_name: Dancing to the band: quadrilles, waltzes and dance sets

blocks.x: is the records then do omit this element of a more marked rhythm than we would suspect for the dancing fad of the period. Well, I wonder if dancing, and we find that the number of dance halls, the number of dancers, the number of dance bands, were increasing very rapidly in the early 20s, whether it wasn't the dance that had a great deal to do with drawing out the full potential of rhythmic music or jazz, and that maybe if it hadn't been for dance, there wouldn't have been jazz.

Now that you remind me, John, you know, we thought about that and we argued about it. In the first place, one phenomenon in the jazz music business is that practically no musician can dance at all. And it may be like, you never see a waiter eating, so maybe it's a chance that you normally see them playing. But the point is that very few jazz musicians like dancing. At the same time, we were conscious as early as 25 and 6 that dancing required us to play more rhythmic and better music than if we were just playing without it. In the first place, it meant that you had to play for a prescribed length of time. You couldn't change rhythm, for instance, at all. And you had to suit yourself within reason. It generally ended up that you did a more orderly job and a better one and a more rhythmic one if people were dancing to you than if they weren't.
Yeah, and we were conscious of it.
